systemPrompt:
You are an expert at planning interactive 3D visualizations for textbook figures.

PRIMARY CONTEXT:
The generated figure will be embedded alongside the original in a PDF reader. It should look recognizably like the source figure — same general geometry, viewpoint, labels, and proportions — but does not need to be a pixel-perfect inline replacement. Some additional controls or layout breathing room are fine if they genuinely help the learner.

INTERACTION PALETTE — choose the interactions that best fit the concept. Pick the fewest that genuinely serve the learning goal; more is not better. In "teaches", say what the learner understands, not what the control does.

• orbit / drag — rotate/move the scene. When depth or 3D shape IS the concept.
• hover — reveal a label on demand. When showing every label at once clutters.
• click — highlight one element. When focus on one part of a busy scene matters.
• slider — sweep one continuous variable. When dragging it visibly transforms the figure.
• toggle — switch between 2+ named views. For before/after or dual views (e.g. spatial ↔ frequency).
• button / state — step through discrete phases. When distinct stages should be visited deliberately.
• animation — self-playing motion. When the concept is inherently dynamic and a slider can't convey it.
• equation_input — learner types math, parsed at runtime. When "change the formula, reshape the output" (integrand, boundary, kernel); each field maps to one curve/quantity; catch parse errors inline.
• code_editor — learner writes/debugs an algorithm; the figure replays its execution frame by frame. Use ONLY when the concept IS a procedure whose intermediate states carry the lesson — heapify, one pass of a sort, a graph traversal, gradient descent, scanline fill — i.e. the question a learner has is "in what order does it touch the data, and why". Needs state small enough to draw whole (~30 elements) and an algorithm expressible in ~20 lines against a handful of operations. Do NOT use it for a continuous parameter (that is a slider), a formula the learner retypes (equation_input), or a static structure with no execution (hover/click). Choose it over animation when the learner should be able to get the procedure WRONG and watch where it diverges.

Output ONLY valid JSON (no markdown, no explanation):
{
  "projection_type": "perspective | axonometric | oblique",
  "camera_view": { "azimuthDeg": <perspective only — 0=side · 45=three-quarter · 90=front-on>, "elevationDeg": <perspective only — 0=eye-level · 20-35=slightly above · 90=top-down>, "rollDeg": 0, "heightFraction": <0.5 default · up to 0.75 to fill the frame> },
  "axis_screen_angles": <axonometric only — null for a flat 2D plot/diagram with no 3D depth (front-on view); omit this field entirely for a 3D axonometric figure (renderer uses a standard isometric pose)>,
  "elements": ["exhaustive list of every geometric element visible in the figure that must be recreated in 3D"],
  "interactions": [
    { "id": "uniqueCamelCaseId", "type": "orbit | drag | hover | click | slider | toggle | button | state | animation | equation_input | code_editor", "teaches": "what the learner understands", "...": "plus ONLY that type's fields — see INTERACTION FIELDS below" }
  ],
  "demo_steps": [
    {
      "title": "Step name shown in UI",
      "narration": "What the learner sees and understands at this step — one or two sentences",
      "state": { "interactionId": value }
    }
  ],
  "geometry_notes": "Approximate world-space scale (e.g. 'cube ~2 units side, axes span ±3'), dominant colors from the source, and any domain-specific formula or value needed for correctness.",
  "notes": "Three.js / rendering technique notes (distinct from geometry_notes)"
}

INTERACTION FIELDS — every interaction object has "id" (unique camelCase), "type", and "teaches". Add ONLY the fields listed for its type; never attach a "range" to anything but a slider.

"type" MUST be exactly one of these 11 strings: "orbit" · "drag" · "hover" · "click" · "slider" · "toggle" · "button" · "state" · "animation" · "equation_input" · "code_editor""

• orbit / drag / hover / click — no extra fields.
• animation      — "label", optional "loop": true | false.
• slider         — "label", "range": [min, max, step], "default": <number>.
• toggle         — "label", "options": ["A", "B", ...], "default": "A"   (a plain on/off toggle may drop "options" and use "default": true | false).
• button / state — "label", "states": ["idle", "running", "done"], "default": "idle".
• equation_input — "label", "fields": [ { "id": "...", "label": "f(x) =", "default": "sin(x)", "variables": ["x"], "domain": [min, max], "role": "integrand | boundary | kernel | ..." } ]. "domain" is the x-range the field is plotted over; always supply it so the generator does not have to guess.
• code_editor    — "label",
                   "entry_point": "the one function the learner must define, e.g. buildMaxHeap(heap)",
                   "api": [ { "op": "greater(i, j)", "does": "true when A[i] > A[j]" }, { "op": "swap(i, j)", "does": "exchange two elements — the ONLY way to mutate" }, ... ],
                   "frame": "what one recorded step shows, e.g. 'the whole array plus the 1-2 indices the op touched'",
                   "input": { "label": "Initial array", "default": "4, 1, 3, 2, 16, 9, 10" },
                   "sample_code": "<correct implementation, as a string>",
                   optional "buggy_code": "<plausible near-miss, with a comment naming the bug>",
                   "success_check": "the property the final state must satisfy, e.g. 'every parent >= both of its children'".
  Design the "api" first and keep it minimal: 4–7 ops covering read, compare, mutate, and annotate (a note/mark op for the learner's own commentary). Every state change must be reachable ONLY through an op — otherwise the replay has gaps. The learner writes algorithm logic, never drawing code.

demo_steps "state" may set values for slider, toggle, and button/state interactions only; code_editor and equation_input are seeded by their sample_code / fields defaults, not by demo_steps.

Rules:
- PROJECTION TYPE: pick whichever the source most resembles. Do not measure angles off the image — the renderer applies a fixed standard pose for each type, so a coarse visual call is enough. Spend your effort on ELEMENTS and INTERACTIONS instead; camera is a quick classification, not a measurement task.
  • "perspective" — depth edges clearly converge toward a vanishing point, or a single object's own far end reads smaller than its near end. Judge within one object; a row of separate same-shape objects that merely shrink (e.g. neural-net layers) is not perspective.
  • "oblique" — one face is drawn true (an undistorted rectangle: right angles, horizontal/vertical edges intact) while depth recedes off it along a single diagonal — e.g. stacked feature maps/filter banks drawn as offset same-size copies.
  • "axonometric" — the default for everything else: any other 3D-looking figure (axes tilted, no true face), or a flat 2D plot/diagram (set "axis_screen_angles": null for these).
- CAMERA VIEW: camera_view sets framing only. azimuthDeg/elevationDeg apply to perspective only: azimuthDeg 0 side, 45 three-quarter, 90 front-on; elevationDeg 0 eye-level, 10–20 low-angle, 25–35 moderate three-quarter, 90 top-down. rollDeg is usually 0. heightFraction is how much of the frame the figure should fill (0.5 default, up to 0.75).
- DEMO STEPS: include when the concept has 2+ distinct phases the learner should visit in sequence, each step driving one named configuration of the interaction state. Use [] for a single continuous exploration with no natural sequence.
- GEOMETRY NOTES: always fill this in — it is what stops the generator guessing sizes and getting the zoom wrong. Cover:
  • world-space dimensions, and for oblique/axonometric figures give each box explicitly as X × Y × Z world units, naming which source dimension each axis carries (+X is screen-right, +Y screen-up, +Z the receding diagonal).
  • the colour palette, with hex codes where determinable from the source.
  • any formula or numeric range the generator needs to be mathematically correct.
  • POSITION AND ORIENTATION for each element as read off the source — which way it points, what angle it sits at, which side of another element it is on. Read this off the image; do not infer layout from general knowledge of the concept. A generic, plausible-looking arrangement is the failure mode the generator falls into whenever geometry_notes covers only dimensions.
  • for a repeated shape with a stated per-element value (channel count, layer size, category), an explicit number for each element's varying dimension tied to that value — equal values get equal size, even across sequence position — rather than a described trend.
- MULTI-PART FIGURES: if the source contains multiple labeled panels ((a)/(b)/(c), side-by-side comparisons, before/after pairs, sequential diagrams), do NOT recreate them all simultaneously in the initial view. Show one panel by default and link the rest through a single interaction — a toggle, tab, or slider — so the learner actively moves between parts. The transition itself should teach the comparison or progression.
- Prefer interactions that expose relationships in the figure rather than generic controls.

Figure: epipolar_geometry

AUTHOR-PROVIDED INTERACTION REQUESTS:
Requested interactions:
- Build the two-camera rig as one live model: the epipolar plane, epipoles e1/e2, and both epipolar lines are recomputed from O1, O2, and P every frame
- Drag the 3D point P: watch p1, p2, the epipolar plane, and both epipolar lines track it continuously
- Drag or rotate camera 2 (sliders for baseline and rotation): the epipoles slide along the image planes and the epipolar lines re-orient, showing the constraint depends only on relative pose

Source file:
visionbook/3d_scene_understanding_stereo.qmd

Use these requested interactions when forming the plan. Use the image to recover visual structure, layout, labels, camera/view cues, and missing visible elements.

Planner context:
This figure illustrates the core geometric relationships in a stereo camera pair. Two cameras with centers O1 and O2 face inward, each with its own image plane; a 3D point P projects to image points p1 and p2 on the respective planes, and the three points O1, P, O2 together define the epipolar plane. The baseline connecting O1 and O2 intersects each image plane at the epipoles e1 and e2, and the intersections of the epipolar plane with each image plane produce the labeled epipolar lines, which pass through the epipoles and through the respective image projections p1 and p2. This constraint means that if p1 is known, the corresponding point p2 must lie somewhere on the epipolar line in the second image, reducing stereo correspondence from a 2D search to a 1D one. The figure establishes the epipolar geometry as the fundamental constraint that links projections across two views, motivating the essential and fundamental matrices.

CONTEXT FROM TEXTBOOK:
This figure illustrates the core geometric relationships in a stereo camera pair. Two cameras with centers O1 and O2 face inward, each with its own image plane; a 3D point P projects to image points p1 and p2 on the respective planes, and the three points O1, P, O2 together define the epipolar plane. The baseline connecting O1 and O2 intersects each image plane at the epipoles e1 and e2, and the intersections of the epipolar plane with each image plane produce the labeled epipolar lines, which pass through the epipoles and through the respective image projections p1 and p2. This constraint means that if p1 is known, the corresponding point p2 must lie somewhere on the epipolar line in the second image, reducing stereo correspondence from a 2D search to a 1D one. The figure establishes the epipolar geometry as the fundamental constraint that links projections across two views, motivating the essential and fundamental matrices.

PROJECTION TYPE: perspective
Use the scaffold's true perspective projection after building all geometry. Use this only when the source has real vanishing-point convergence or distance-based size shrinkage; then depth should visibly affect apparent size.

ELEMENTS TO RECREATE IN 3D:
  - Camera 1 center O1 — large black sphere at far left, sitting on the baseline
  - Camera 2 center O2 — large black sphere at far right, sitting on the baseline
  - Image plane 1 — dark-gray outlined quadrilateral (parallelogram in projection) standing in front of O1, tilted so it recedes to the lower-right; O1 appears at its left edge
  - Image plane 2 — dark-gray outlined quadrilateral in front of O2, mirror-tilted, receding to the lower-left; O2 appears at its right edge
  - 3D scene point P — small cyan filled circle with black outline, high above and slightly left of center
  - Ray O1→P — thick red segment passing through image plane 1 at p1
  - Ray O2→P — thick red segment passing through image plane 2 at p2
  - Baseline O1—O2 — heavy black dashed horizontal line across the whole figure
  - Epipolar plane — large translucent yellow triangle with vertices O1, P, O2 (its interior fills the middle of the figure)
  - Pale-yellow sub-wedges where the epipolar plane passes through each image plane quad (lighter tint region inside each plane)
  - Pink/magenta highlight stripe where the epipolar plane crosses the upper edge region of each image plane
  - Epipole e1 — small black dot where the baseline pierces image plane 1
  - Epipole e2 — small black dot where the baseline pierces image plane 2
  - Projected point p1 — red dot with black ring on image plane 1
  - Projected point p2 — red dot with black ring on image plane 2
  - Epipolar line in image 1 — thin red line through e1 and p1, extending to the plane borders
  - Epipolar line in image 2 — thin red line through e2 and p2, extending to the plane borders
  - Camera 1 image-axes — two green arrows (one up, one to the upper-left) drawn on image plane 1, plus a faint green in-plane guide line from e1
  - Camera 2 image-axes — two blue arrows (one up, one to the lower-left) drawn on image plane 2, plus a thin blue in-plane guide line from e2
  - Text labels: P, p1, p2, e1, e2, O1, O2, 'Camera 1' (far left), 'Camera 2' (far right), 'Epipolar plane' (inside the yellow triangle), 'Epipolar line' rotated along each red image line

GEOMETRY NOTES (world-space scale, color palette, and any formula/value needed for correctness — build to these so sizes, zoom, and colors match the source; do not guess dimensions the notes already specify):
World units: baseline along +X. O1 = (-4, 0, 0), O2 = (+4, 0, 0) at default baseline 8 (slider scales both symmetrically about the origin). Camera centers drawn as black spheres r = 0.28. Focal distance f = 1.9: each image plane is a flat rectangle 3.6 wide (local u) × 2.8 tall (local v, +Y up), centered on its optical axis at distance f in front of its center, so the baseline pierces plane 1 at e1 = O1 + f·d1_x-component and plane 2 at e2 likewise. Default optical axes point inward and slightly toward the viewer: d1 = normalize(+1, 0, +0.35) yawed so plane 1 shows its front-left face (matches source: plane 1 recedes down-right, O1 on its left edge); d2 = normalize(-1, 0, +0.35) yawed by cam2Yaw (default -20°, mirror pose so plane 2 recedes down-left, O2 on its right edge). Both planes have local v = world +Y (no roll). Scene point P default (-0.7, 3.6, -1.2); drag domain x∈[-3,3], y∈[1.2,5], z∈[-3,2.5] — P stays above the baseline so the epipolar plane reads as the tall yellow triangle. p_i = intersection of segment O_i→P with image plane i; epipolar line i = intersection of plane(O1,P,O2) with image plane i, clipped to the plane rectangle. Colors from source: epipolar plane fill pure yellow #FFFF00 at ~0.55 opacity (double-sided, no lighting); rays O1P/O2P and plane edge lines heavy red #FF0000 (line width ~4–5 px); thin epipolar lines red #FF0000 (~2 px); image-plane borders dark gray #3A3A3A (~3 px); baseline black #000000 dashed (dash 0.28, gap 0.22, ~4 px); P cyan #59E6E6 with black ring; p1/p2 red #FF0000 with black ring, r≈0.10; e1/e2 solid black r≈0.09; camera-1 in-plane axis arrows green #00C000 (one pointing +v up, one pointing up-left along -u); camera-2 in-plane axis arrows blue #2A7FFF (one +v up, one down-left along -u) plus one thin blue in-plane line through e2; pale-yellow tint #FFFFB0 (~0.4) for the sub-wedge where the epipolar plane crosses each image rectangle, with a short pink #FFB6D0 stripe at the upper crossing edge. Labels in serif, black, bold for P/p1/p2/O1/O2/e1/e2; 'Epipolar plane' centered in the yellow triangle; 'Epipolar line' rotated to run along each red image line; 'Camera 1' left of O1, 'Camera 2' right of O2 slightly above.

DISCRETE CONTROLS (implement every one of these in #ui, each must work independently):

    "type": "orbit",
    "teaches": "The epipolar plane is a genuine 3D plane through O1, P and O2 — rotating the rig shows the image-plane 'lines' are just its intersections with the two sensors, not drawn-on decorations."

    "type": "drag",

    "type": "slider",
    "label": "Baseline |O1O2|",
    "range": [

    "default": 8,

  },
  {
    "id": "cam2Yaw",
    "type": "slider",
    "label": "Camera 2 rotation (yaw°)",
    "range": [
      -45,
      45,
      1
    ],
    "default": -20,
    "teaches": "Rotating camera 2 re-orients its image plane, so e2 shifts and the epipolar line in image 2 changes direction — the epipolar constraint is fixed by relative pose (R, t) alone."
  },
  {
    "id": "viewMode",
    "type": "toggle",
    "label": "View",
    "options": [
      "3D rig",
      "Camera 2 image"
    ],
    "default": "3D rig",
    "teaches": "Seen face-on from camera 2, the epipolar line reduces the search for the match of p1 from the whole 2D image to a single 1D line through e2."
  }
]

DEMO STEPS (tween through these using goToStep(); each step drives the controls above):
[
  {
    "title": "The two-view rig",
    "narration": "Two camera centers O1 and O2 with their image planes face inward; the dashed baseline joins them and pierces each plane at the epipoles e1 and e2.",
    "state": {
      "baseline": 8,
      "cam2Yaw": -20,
      "viewMode": "3D rig"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "One point, one plane",
    "narration": "The scene point P plus the two centers span the yellow epipolar plane; the red rays O1P and O2P lie in it and pierce the sensors at p1 and p2.",
    "state": {
      "baseline": 8,
      "cam2Yaw": -20,
      "viewMode": "3D rig"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Epipolar lines are intersections",
    "narration": "Where the yellow plane cuts each image plane you get the epipolar line — it necessarily passes through both the epipole and the projected point.",
    "state": {
      "baseline": 8,
      "cam2Yaw": -20,
      "viewMode": "3D rig"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Change the relative pose",
    "narration": "Shrinking the baseline and rotating camera 2 slides the epipoles and swings the epipolar lines, while p1, p2 remain on them: the constraint is set by relative pose only.",
    "state": {
      "baseline": 4.5,
      "cam2Yaw": 30,
      "viewMode": "3D rig"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "2D search becomes 1D",
    "narration": "Looking straight into camera 2's image, the match for p1 can only lie along the single epipolar line through e2.",
    "state": {
      "baseline": 8,
      "cam2Yaw": -20,
      "viewMode": "Camera 2 image"
    }
  }

CAMERA VIEW (framing only). Call setCameraView({ projection, ...these }) AFTER all geometry is added. Keep the projection MECHANISM from PROJECTION TYPE above (orthographic / sheared-oblique / perspective). For perspective these params set the pose (azimuth/elevation/roll); for the two parallel projections pose is a standard default (see PROJECTION TYPE above), and these params set only roll and framing (heightFraction):
{
  "azimuthDeg": 12,
  "elevationDeg": 14,
  "rollDeg": 0,
  "heightFraction": 0.68
}

NOTES: Build everything procedurally each frame from O1, O2, P and the two camera poses — no baked geometry. Epipolar plane: normal n = (P-O1)×(P-O2) normalized; render the triangle O1-P-O2 with THREE.DoubleSide, depthWrite false, transparent, and render it after the opaque planes so the yellow reads over the background but the red rays (drawn with polygonOffset / slightly larger renderOrder) stay visible. Compute epipolar lines by clipping the plane–plane intersection ray against the 3.6×2.8 image rectangle in local (u,v) coords (Liang–Barsky); rebuild the LineSegments positions in place. Use Line2/LineMaterial (fat lines) for the red rays, plane borders and dashed baseline so widths match the heavy strokes in the source at any zoom; dashed baseline via LineDashedMaterial with computeLineDistances or Line2 dashed. Labels as CSS2DRenderer/sprite HTML so the rotated 'Epipolar line' text can be CSS-rotated and stays legible while orbiting; label anchors update from projected positions. Drag P with a plane-constrained pointer handler (TransformControls-free): raycast against a plane through P parallel to the screen, with Shift to move along Z; clamp to the stated domain. 'Camera 2 image' toggle animates the camera to the -d2 direction, orthographic-ish framing of image plane 2, and fades out the yellow plane while keeping the epipolar line, e2, p2 and a highlighted 1D search band. Keep an axes-arrow helper built from ArrowHelper for the green/blue in-plane axes, re-parented to each image plane's local frame.

Follow the interaction plan above.

CONTEXT FROM TEXTBOOK:
This figure illustrates the core geometric relationships in a stereo camera pair. Two cameras with centers O1 and O2 face inward, each with its own image plane; a 3D point P projects to image points p1 and p2 on the respective planes, and the three points O1, P, O2 together define the epipolar plane. The baseline connecting O1 and O2 intersects each image plane at the epipoles e1 and e2, and the intersections of the epipolar plane with each image plane produce the labeled epipolar lines, which pass through the epipoles and through the respective image projections p1 and p2. This constraint means that if p1 is known, the corresponding point p2 must lie somewhere on the epipolar line in the second image, reducing stereo correspondence from a 2D search to a 1D one. The figure establishes the epipolar geometry as the fundamental constraint that links projections across two views, motivating the essential and fundamental matrices.

PROJECTION TYPE: perspective
Use the scaffold's true perspective projection after building all geometry. Use this only when the source has real vanishing-point convergence or distance-based size shrinkage; then depth should visibly affect apparent size.

ELEMENTS TO RECREATE IN 3D:
  - Camera 1 center O1 — large black sphere at far left, sitting on the baseline
  - Camera 2 center O2 — large black sphere at far right, sitting on the baseline
  - Image plane 1 — dark-gray outlined quadrilateral (parallelogram in projection) standing in front of O1, tilted so it recedes to the lower-right; O1 appears at its left edge
  - Image plane 2 — dark-gray outlined quadrilateral in front of O2, mirror-tilted, receding to the lower-left; O2 appears at its right edge
  - 3D scene point P — small cyan filled circle with black outline, high above and slightly left of center
  - Ray O1→P — thick red segment passing through image plane 1 at p1
  - Ray O2→P — thick red segment passing through image plane 2 at p2
  - Baseline O1—O2 — heavy black dashed horizontal line across the whole figure
  - Epipolar plane — large translucent yellow triangle with vertices O1, P, O2 (its interior fills the middle of the figure)
  - Pale-yellow sub-wedges where the epipolar plane passes through each image plane quad (lighter tint region inside each plane)
  - Pink/magenta highlight stripe where the epipolar plane crosses the upper edge region of each image plane
  - Epipole e1 — small black dot where the baseline pierces image plane 1
  - Epipole e2 — small black dot where the baseline pierces image plane 2
  - Projected point p1 — red dot with black ring on image plane 1
  - Projected point p2 — red dot with black ring on image plane 2
  - Epipolar line in image 1 — thin red line through e1 and p1, extending to the plane borders
  - Epipolar line in image 2 — thin red line through e2 and p2, extending to the plane borders
  - Camera 1 image-axes — two green arrows (one up, one to the upper-left) drawn on image plane 1, plus a faint green in-plane guide line from e1
  - Camera 2 image-axes — two blue arrows (one up, one to the lower-left) drawn on image plane 2, plus a thin blue in-plane guide line from e2
  - Text labels: P, p1, p2, e1, e2, O1, O2, 'Camera 1' (far left), 'Camera 2' (far right), 'Epipolar plane' (inside the yellow triangle), 'Epipolar line' rotated along each red image line

GEOMETRY NOTES (world-space scale, color palette, and any formula/value needed for correctness — build to these so sizes, zoom, and colors match the source; do not guess dimensions the notes already specify):
World units: baseline along +X. O1 = (-4, 0, 0), O2 = (+4, 0, 0) at default baseline 8 (slider scales both symmetrically about the origin). Camera centers drawn as black spheres r = 0.28. Focal distance f = 1.9: each image plane is a flat rectangle 3.6 wide (local u) × 2.8 tall (local v, +Y up), centered on its optical axis at distance f in front of its center, so the baseline pierces plane 1 at e1 = O1 + f·d1_x-component and plane 2 at e2 likewise. Default optical axes point inward and slightly toward the viewer: d1 = normalize(+1, 0, +0.35) yawed so plane 1 shows its front-left face (matches source: plane 1 recedes down-right, O1 on its left edge); d2 = normalize(-1, 0, +0.35) yawed by cam2Yaw (default -20°, mirror pose so plane 2 recedes down-left, O2 on its right edge). Both planes have local v = world +Y (no roll). Scene point P default (-0.7, 3.6, -1.2); drag domain x∈[-3,3], y∈[1.2,5], z∈[-3,2.5] — P stays above the baseline so the epipolar plane reads as the tall yellow triangle. p_i = intersection of segment O_i→P with image plane i; epipolar line i = intersection of plane(O1,P,O2) with image plane i, clipped to the plane rectangle. Colors from source: epipolar plane fill pure yellow #FFFF00 at ~0.55 opacity (double-sided, no lighting); rays O1P/O2P and plane edge lines heavy red #FF0000 (line width ~4–5 px); thin epipolar lines red #FF0000 (~2 px); image-plane borders dark gray #3A3A3A (~3 px); baseline black #000000 dashed (dash 0.28, gap 0.22, ~4 px); P cyan #59E6E6 with black ring; p1/p2 red #FF0000 with black ring, r≈0.10; e1/e2 solid black r≈0.09; camera-1 in-plane axis arrows green #00C000 (one pointing +v up, one pointing up-left along -u); camera-2 in-plane axis arrows blue #2A7FFF (one +v up, one down-left along -u) plus one thin blue in-plane line through e2; pale-yellow tint #FFFFB0 (~0.4) for the sub-wedge where the epipolar plane crosses each image rectangle, with a short pink #FFB6D0 stripe at the upper crossing edge. Labels in serif, black, bold for P/p1/p2/O1/O2/e1/e2; 'Epipolar plane' centered in the yellow triangle; 'Epipolar line' rotated to run along each red image line; 'Camera 1' left of O1, 'Camera 2' right of O2 slightly above.

DISCRETE CONTROLS (implement every one of these in #ui, each must work independently):
[
  {
    "id": "orbitRig",
    "type": "orbit",
    "teaches": "The epipolar plane is a genuine 3D plane through O1, P and O2 — rotating the rig shows the image-plane 'lines' are just its intersections with the two sensors, not drawn-on decorations."
  },
  {
    "id": "dragP",
    "type": "drag",
    "teaches": "Moving the scene point P swings the whole epipolar plane about the fixed baseline: p1 and p2 slide, but each stays on its epipolar line, which always pivots about the fixed epipole."
  },
  {
    "id": "baseline",
    "type": "slider",
    "label": "Baseline |O1O2|",
    "range": [
      3,
      10,
      0.1
    ],
    "default": 8,
    "teaches": "Widening or narrowing the baseline moves the epipoles along each image plane and changes the tilt of the epipolar plane — the constraint geometry depends on relative camera position, not on the scene."
  },
  {
    "id": "cam2Yaw",
    "type": "slider",
    "label": "Camera 2 rotation (yaw°)",
    "range": [
      -45,
      45,
      1
    ],
    "default": -20,
    "teaches": "Rotating camera 2 re-orients its image plane, so e2 shifts and the epipolar line in image 2 changes direction — the epipolar constraint is fixed by relative pose (R, t) alone."
  },
  {
    "id": "viewMode",
    "type": "toggle",
    "label": "View",
    "options": [
      "3D rig",
      "Camera 2 image"
    ],
    "default": "3D rig",
    "teaches": "Seen face-on from camera 2, the epipolar line reduces the search for the match of p1 from the whole 2D image to a single 1D line through e2."
  }
]

DEMO STEPS (tween through these using goToStep(); each step drives the controls above):

  {
    "title": "The two-view rig",
    "narration": "Two camera centers O1 and O2 with their image planes face inward; the dashed baseline joins them and pierces each plane at the epipoles e1 and e2.",

  },

    "narration": "The scene point P plus the two centers span the yellow epipolar plane; the red rays O1P and O2P lie in it and pierce the sensors at p1 and p2.",

      "baseline": 8,
      "cam2Yaw": -20,
      "viewMode": "3D rig"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Epipolar lines are intersections",
    "narration": "Where the yellow plane cuts each image plane you get the epipolar line — it necessarily passes through both the epipole and the projected point.",
    "state": {
      "baseline": 8,
      "cam2Yaw": -20,
      "viewMode": "3D rig"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Change the relative pose",
    "narration": "Shrinking the baseline and rotating camera 2 slides the epipoles and swings the epipolar lines, while p1, p2 remain on them: the constraint is set by relative pose only.",
    "state": {
      "baseline": 4.5,
      "cam2Yaw": 30,
      "viewMode": "3D rig"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "2D search becomes 1D",
    "narration": "Looking straight into camera 2's image, the match for p1 can only lie along the single epipolar line through e2.",
    "state": {
      "baseline": 8,
      "cam2Yaw": -20,
      "viewMode": "Camera 2 image"
    }
  }
]

CAMERA VIEW (framing only). Call setCameraView({ projection, ...these }) AFTER all geometry is added. Keep the projection MECHANISM from PROJECTION TYPE above (orthographic / sheared-oblique / perspective). For perspective these params set the pose (azimuth/elevation/roll); for the two parallel projections pose is a standard default (see PROJECTION TYPE above), and these params set only roll and framing (heightFraction):
{
  "azimuthDeg": 12,
  "elevationDeg": 14,
  "rollDeg": 0,
  "heightFraction": 0.68
}

NOTES: Build everything procedurally each frame from O1, O2, P and the two camera poses — no baked geometry. Epipolar plane: normal n = (P-O1)×(P-O2) normalized; render the triangle O1-P-O2 with THREE.DoubleSide, depthWrite false, transparent, and render it after the opaque planes so the yellow reads over the background but the red rays (drawn with polygonOffset / slightly larger renderOrder) stay visible. Compute epipolar lines by clipping the plane–plane intersection ray against the 3.6×2.8 image rectangle in local (u,v) coords (Liang–Barsky); rebuild the LineSegments positions in place. Use Line2/LineMaterial (fat lines) for the red rays, plane borders and dashed baseline so widths match the heavy strokes in the source at any zoom; dashed baseline via LineDashedMaterial with computeLineDistances or Line2 dashed. Labels as CSS2DRenderer/sprite HTML so the rotated 'Epipolar line' text can be CSS-rotated and stays legible while orbiting; label anchors update from projected positions. Drag P with a plane-constrained pointer handler (TransformControls-free): raycast against a plane through P parallel to the screen, with Shift to move along Z; clamp to the stated domain. 'Camera 2 image' toggle animates the camera to the -d2 direction, orthographic-ish framing of image plane 2, and fades out the yellow plane while keeping the epipolar line, e2, p2 and a highlighted 1D search band. Keep an axes-arrow helper built from ArrowHelper for the green/blue in-plane axes, re-parented to each image plane's local frame.
